nodes.name: WOx/piperazine synthesis
nodes.procedure: First, 1 mmol of ammonium metatungstate hydrate was dissolved in 40 mL of distilled water. Then, 9 mmol of piperazine hexahydrate was added into the above solution. After magnetic stirring for 10 min at room temperature, hydrochloric acid solution (1 mol L^{-1}) was added drop-wise until a white precipitate appeared at pH of ≈7. The as-prepared precipitates were aged at 50°C for 6 h. After filtration, the precipitates were washed with distilled water and ethanol for three times, respectively. Finally, WOx/piperazine precursor was obtained after drying at 50°C for 12 h.

nodes.name: Pt/WO3 pyrolysis at 400°C
nodes.procedure: First, 50 mg WOx/piperazine was dispersed in 20 mL absolute ethyl alcohol in a vial and sonicated for 10 min. After that, 320 μL H2PtCl6 solution (0.05 mol L^{-1}) was added into the above dispersion. And, the mixture was magnetically stirred for 3 h. Then, the suspension was separated by centrifugation and dried at 50°C. Finally, the solid powder was pyrolyzed at 400°C for 5 h under Ar atmosphere with a heating rate of 1°C min^{-1}.

nodes.description: HER stability at 400 mA/cm² in 0.5 M H2SO4
nodes.source_text: its durability test was further measured at a large current density of 400 mA cm−2 in 0.5 M H2SO4. As depicted in Figure S15b (Supporting Information), the potential of this electrocatalyst keeps steady during the 65 h acidic HER process.
The Pt/WO3-600 delivers negligible variation even after 2000 continuously repeated LSV (Figure S15a, Supporting Information).

nodes.characterization_summary: All Pt/WO3 samples display cubic WO3 structure (JCPDS 46-1096) with increasing crystallinity from 400-600°C; weak Pt peaks observed in Pt/WO3-500 and Pt/WO3-600.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The crystal structure was first investigated via X-ray diffraction (XRD) and the series of Pt/WO3 with varying pyrolysis temperatures all display the cubic WO3 structure (JCPDS 46-1096) (Figure 2a).

nodes.characterization_summary: All samples show characteristic cubic WO3 peaks at 257, 703, and 801 cm⁻¹ with increasing intensity and decreasing FWHM at 801 cm⁻¹ with higher pyrolysis temperature.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Raman spectra (Figure 2b) of three samples all share similar characteristic peaks of cubic WO3 at 257, 703, and 801 cm⁻¹.

nodes.characterization_summary: All Pt/WO3 samples exhibit similar 1D nanorod structure inherited from WO_x/piperazine hybrid.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) results reveal that three samples all exhibit similar nanorods structure (Figure 2c-e).

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt contents are 3.19 wt%, 3.21 wt%, and 4.23 wt% for Pt/WO3-400, Pt/WO3-500, and Pt/WO3-600 respectively.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The corresponding Pt contents are 3.19, 3.21, and 4.23 wt% for Pt/WO3-400, Pt/WO3-500, and Pt/WO3-600, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt/WO3-600 shows nanorods of ~5 nm WO3 nanocrystals with uniformly dispersed Pt nanoclusters (0.376 nm (200) fringes) and some aggregated Pt nanoparticles.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Among Pt/WO3-600, the WO3 support is composed of ca. 5 nm WO3 nanocrystals (Figure 3b) ... with (200) lattice fringes of 0.376 nm identified in Pt/WO3-600 (Figure 3b).

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt/WO3-600 shows larger Pt nanoparticles with 0.226 nm (111) lattice spacing; average sizes of Pt nanoclusters and nanoparticles are 1.3 nm and 5.3 nm respectively.
nodes.evidence_snippet: some larger size Pt nanoparticles are also found in Pt aggregated region, presenting 0.226 nm crystalline lattice attributed to the (111) facet of Pt (Figure 3c-e).

nodes.characterization_summary: W and O uniformly distributed on WO3 nanorods; Pt distributed throughout with some aggregation in Pt/WO3-600.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Figure 3f-i, W and O elements both uniformly distribute on WO3 nanorods. For Pt element, it is distributed throughout the nanorods, but some regions exhibit aggregation.

nodes.characterization_summary: O 1s shows increasing lattice oxygen vacancy-related O_OH species (9.6%, 17.5%, 30.5% for Pt/WO3-400, -500, -600); Pt 4f binding energy shifts to lower values with increasing pyrolysis temperature; Pt⁰ fractions 47.8%, 52.0%, 67.9% and average valences +1.52, +1.25, +0.85 respectively.
nodes.evidence_snippet: With increasing the pyrolysis temperature, the fraction of O_OH group is 9.6% 17.5% and 30.5% respectively, for Pt/WO3-400 Pt/WO3-500, and Pt/WO3-600 ... the Pt⁰ fraction of Pt/WO3-400, Pt/WO3-500, and Pt/WO3-600 is 47.8% 52.0% and 67.9% respectively. Accordingly, the average valence state of Pt species for these three samples is +1.52 +1.25 and +0.85

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt/WO3-600 shows smallest charge transfer resistance R_ct of 15 Ω.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Pt/WO3-600 presents the smallest charge transfer resistance (R_ct) of only 15Ω without adding conductive carbon power.

nodes.characterization_summary: Work function decreases from 6.57 eV to 2.93 eV with increasing pyrolysis temperature, indicating better charge transfer ability for Pt/WO3-600.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As depicted in Figure S10a-c (Supporting Information), the work function is negatively shifted from 6.57 to 2.93 eV with increasing the pyrolysis temperature.

nodes.characterization_summary: Pt/WO3-600 shows lower Mott-Schottky slope than Pt/WO3-400 and -500, implying improved conductivity.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In addition, the lower Mott-Schottky slope of Pt/WO3-600 with respect to Pt/WO3-400 and Pt/WO3-500 implies its improved conductivity (Figure S11, Supporting Information).
